certification.title: Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer
certification.description: Deploy applications, monitor operations, and manage enterprise solutions on Google Cloud Platform.

exam_versions.change_summary: Updated to reflect GKE Autopilot, Cloud Run, and Vertex AI tooling.

domains.title: Setting Up a Cloud Solution Environment
domains.description: Set up cloud projects and accounts, manage billing, and install and configure the Cloud SDK.

objectives.title: Setting up cloud projects and accounts
objectives.description: Create and manage projects with the Resource Manager hierarchy (Organization, Folders, Projects). Configure IAM policies, service accounts, and Workload Identity Federation. Enable and disable APIs per project.

skills.title: Creating and Managing Google Cloud Projects
skills.description: Organize resources using projects, folders, and organization hierarchy nodes.

objectives.title: Managing billing configuration
objectives.description: Create and manage billing accounts and link them to projects. Establish billing budgets and alerts. Export billing data to BigQuery for analysis.

skills.title: Manage Cloud Billing Accounts and Budgets
skills.description: Configure billing accounts, project linkages, budgets, and automated alerts.

objectives.title: Installing and configuring the command line interface (CLI)
objectives.description: Install the Google Cloud CLI (gcloud). Initialize and configure named configurations. Switch between projects and accounts. Use Cloud Shell as a browser-based alternative.

skills.title: Installing and Initializing the Google Cloud CLI
skills.description: Install gcloud, manage named configurations, and execute core commands.

domains.title: Planning and Configuring a Cloud Solution
domains.description: Plan and estimate using the Pricing Calculator, plan and configure compute, data storage, and network resources.

objectives.title: Planning and estimating Google Cloud product use using the Pricing Calculator
objectives.description: Estimate costs for Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Cloud SQL. Understand sustained use discounts, committed use discounts, and preemptible VM pricing.

skills.title: Sustained and Committed Use Discounts
skills.description: Evaluate automated sustained use discounts and resource commitments.

objectives.title: Planning and configuring compute resources
objectives.description: Select appropriate Compute Engine machine types (general-purpose, compute-optimized, memory-optimized). Choose between GCE, GKE, App Engine, Cloud Run, and Cloud Functions based on workload requirements.

skills.title: Compute Engine Machine Series and Types
skills.description: Choose between general-purpose, compute-optimized, and accelerator machine families.

objectives.title: Planning and configuring data storage options
objectives.description: Choose between Cloud Storage (object), Cloud SQL (relational), Cloud Spanner (globally distributed relational), Firestore (NoSQL document), Bigtable (wide-column NoSQL), and BigQuery (analytics warehouse).

skills.title: Cloud Storage Storage Classes and Lifecycle
skills.description: Select Standard, Nearline, Coldline, or Archive storage classes based on access frequency.

objectives.title: Planning and configuring network resources
objectives.description: Differentiate load balancing options (global HTTP(S), TCP/SSL proxy, regional Network, internal). Configure Cloud DNS, Cloud CDN, Cloud VPN, and Cloud Interconnect. Design VPC networks with subnets and firewall rules.

skills.title: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Network Design
skills.description: Configure subnets, routes, firewall rules, and VPC peering.

domains.title: Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
domains.description: Deploy and implement Compute Engine, GKE, App Engine, Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and data/storage solutions.

objectives.title: Deploying and implementing Compute Engine resources
objectives.description: Create VM instances using the Console and gcloud CLI. Configure startup scripts, metadata, and labels. Attach persistent and local SSDs. Create managed instance groups with autoscaling and health checks.

skills.title: Create and Start Compute Engine VM Instances
skills.description: Provision VMs, configure metadata and startup scripts via gcloud compute instances create.

objectives.title: Deploying and implementing Google Kubernetes Engine resources
objectives.description: Deploy GKE clusters in Standard and Autopilot mode. Deploy containerized workloads using kubectl and YAML manifests. Configure horizontal pod autoscalers, node pools, and cluster upgrades.

skills.title: Deploy Containerized Apps to GKE Clusters
skills.description: Create GKE clusters and deploy container workloads with kubectl.

objectives.title: Deploying and implementing Cloud Run and Cloud Functions resources
objectives.description: Deploy stateless containerized services to Cloud Run. Write and deploy event-driven Cloud Functions (1st and 2nd gen). Configure triggers, concurrency, min/max instances, and VPC connectors.

skills.title: Deploy Services to Cloud Run
skills.description: Build and deploy container images to serverless Cloud Run services.

objectives.title: Deploying and implementing data solutions
objectives.description: Initialize Cloud SQL instances and configure failover replicas. Load data into BigQuery via batch and streaming. Create and manage Cloud Storage buckets with appropriate storage classes (Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive).

skills.title: Create and Manage Cloud SQL Instances
skills.description: Provision managed PostgreSQL/MySQL instances, high availability, and backups.

domains.title: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
domains.description: Manage Compute Engine and GKE resources, configure Cloud Monitoring and Logging, and manage networking and storage.

objectives.title: Managing Compute Engine resources
objectives.description: Manage VM states (start, stop, suspend, reset). Take snapshots and create machine images. Resize VMs and migrate instances. Use SSH, OS Login, and Serial Console for access.

skills.title: Managing Compute Engine VM Lifecycle and Snapshots
skills.description: Control instance power states, create persistent disk snapshots, and resize resources.

objectives.title: Managing Google Kubernetes Engine resources
objectives.description: View current running cluster inventory (pods, nodes, services). Browse Docker images in Artifact Registry. Work with kubectl to apply, rollout, and scale deployments. Manage persistent volumes and ConfigMaps.

skills.title: Scaling and Managing GKE Workloads
skills.description: Scale deployments, execute rollouts, and inspect cluster health using kubectl.

objectives.title: Managing Cloud Run resources
objectives.description: Adjust application traffic splitting between revisions. Deploy new revisions and roll back. Set environment variables, secrets (via Secret Manager), and concurrency limits.

skills.title: Traffic Management and Revision Splitting on Cloud Run
skills.description: Split traffic across multiple service revisions for canary and blue/green deployments.

objectives.title: Managing monitoring and logging
objectives.description: Create Cloud Monitoring dashboards with metrics, charts, and alerts. Configure log-based metrics and log sinks to Cloud Storage or BigQuery. Use Cloud Trace and Cloud Profiler for performance analysis.

skills.title: Cloud Monitoring Dashboards, Alerts, and Log Sinks
skills.description: Build custom metric dashboards, alert policies, and export audit logs.

domains.title: Configuring Access and Security
domains.description: Manage IAM, service accounts, and audit logs.

objectives.title: Managing Identity and Access Management (IAM)
objectives.description: Assign predefined and custom IAM roles at the organization, folder, and project level. Understand role inheritance, deny policies, and the principle of least privilege. Use IAM Conditions for context-aware access.

skills.title: Understanding and Assigning Google Cloud IAM Roles
skills.description: Configure predefined, custom, and conditional IAM roles across resource hierarchy.

objectives.title: Managing service accounts
objectives.description: Create and manage service accounts. Assign service accounts to VM instances and Cloud Run services. Use Workload Identity Federation to allow external workloads to impersonate service accounts without keys.

skills.title: Creating and Managing Service Accounts and Keyless Access
skills.description: Provision service accounts, configure least privilege, and attach to compute resources.

objectives.title: Viewing audit logs
objectives.description: Distinguish between Admin Activity, Data Access, System Event, and Policy Denied audit logs. Export audit logs using log sinks. Understand which audit log types are enabled by default and which require explicit activation.

skills.title: Google Cloud Audit Logs Overview and Configuration
skills.description: Analyze Admin Activity, Data Access, and System Event audit logs in Cloud Logging.

practice_questions.stem: You are designing the Google Cloud resource hierarchy for an enterprise with multiple business units. You need to ensure that security policies and compliance constraints (such as disabling external IP addresses on VMs) can be enforced centrally across all projects in the engineering department without preventing other departments from using external IPs. How should you structure the hierarchy?

options.text: Create an Organization Policy constraint directly at the Organization node.
options.explanation: Applying the constraint at the Organization node would affect all departments, violating the requirement.

options.text: Create a Folder for the Engineering department, place all engineering projects within this folder, and apply the Organization Policy constraint to the Engineering folder.
options.explanation: Correct. Organization policies inherit down the resource hierarchy (Organization -> Folder -> Project). Applying the constraint at the Engineering folder enforces compliance for all engineering projects while leaving other folders unaffected.

options.text: Apply individual VPC firewall rules on each VM inside the engineering projects.
options.explanation: Firewall rules manage traffic at the network level and cannot prevent developers from assigning public IP addresses during VM creation.

options.text: Assign the Compute Security Admin role to each engineering project individually.
options.explanation: IAM roles grant authorization to users, but do not programmatically prevent VM configuration violations like organization policies do.

practice_questions.explanation: Resource Manager Folders allow grouping projects to centrally administer IAM permissions and Organization Policies. Constraints defined at the Folder level are inherited by all child projects within that folder without affecting sibling folders.

practice_questions.stem: Your company has multiple Google Cloud projects linked to a central Cloud Billing account. The finance team requires an alert when the monthly cloud spend reaches 90% of the $10,000 budget. They also want to programmatically shut down test environment VMs if the budget reaches 100%. What should you configure?

options.text: Configure a billing budget of $10,000 with email alerts at 90%, and configure a Pub/Sub notification channel connected to a Cloud Function to shut down test VMs at 100%.
options.explanation: Correct. Cloud Billing budgets support email notifications at threshold percentages and can publish budget events to Pub/Sub topics to trigger serverless automation (Cloud Function / Cloud Run) to stop non-production resources.

options.text: Set a hard spending cap in the Cloud Billing console to automatically freeze all project APIs at 100%.
options.explanation: Google Cloud Billing budgets do NOT provide an automatic built-in hard-cap switch; automation must be triggered via Pub/Sub.

options.text: Use Cloud Monitoring uptime checks to measure API billing metrics and trigger automated VM termination.
options.explanation: Uptime checks test HTTP/TCP availability, not billing account spend.

options.text: Export billing data to BigQuery every 5 minutes and run a scheduled query to terminate VMs via gcloud.
options.explanation: Billing data export to BigQuery occurs multiple times a day with batch latency, not in real-time.

practice_questions.explanation: Billing budgets send email alerts to Billing Admins by default. To take automated programmatic action (e.g. disabling billing or stopping test VMs), link the budget to a Cloud Pub/Sub topic and invoke a Cloud Function handler.

practice_questions.stem: You regularly work across three separate Google Cloud projects (development, staging, and production) with different user accounts, compute zones, and default settings. What is the most efficient way to manage and switch between these configurations using the Google Cloud CLI?

options.text: Run `gcloud init` every time you need to switch environments.
options.explanation: Running `gcloud init` each time requires going through the full interactive authentication flow.

options.text: Create a named configuration for each environment using `gcloud config configurations create <name>` and switch between them using `gcloud config configurations activate <name>`.
options.explanation: Correct. Named configurations store distinct sets of properties (account, project, region, zone) and allow instant switching without re-authenticating.

options.text: Uninstall and reinstall the Google Cloud CLI in different directories on your machine.
options.explanation: Multiple CLI installations are unnecessary and difficult to maintain.

options.text: Set environment variables `CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT` manually in your shell for every single gcloud command.
options.explanation: Manual environment variables are error-prone and do not manage accounts or regional defaults cleanly.

practice_questions.explanation: The Google Cloud CLI supports named configurations (`gcloud config configurations create/activate/list`) which encapsulate account credentials, default project IDs, and compute regions for fast context switching.

practice_questions.stem: You are planning the deployment of a stateless web processing workload on Compute Engine that will run continuously 24/7 for the entire year. The application requires predictable CPU and RAM performance. What is the most cost-effective pricing mechanism?

options.text: Use On-Demand VMs with automatic Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs).
options.explanation: SUDs provide up to 30% discount, but Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) offer substantially higher discounts for predictable 1-year or 3-year workloads.

options.text: Purchase a 1-year or 3-year Committed Use Discount (CUD) for the required compute resources.
options.explanation: Correct. For steady-state workloads running continuously for a known duration of 1 or 3 years, CUDs provide the deepest discount (up to 57% for standard instances and 70% for memory-optimized) without upfront licensing fees.

options.text: Use Spot VM instances for all web processing nodes.
options.explanation: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with 30 seconds notice, making them unsuitable as the sole foundation for a continuous production web workload.

options.text: Use sole-tenant nodes with per-minute billing.
options.explanation: Sole-tenant nodes carry a 10% premium over standard pricing and are intended for compliance/isolation needs.

practice_questions.explanation: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) are ideal for workloads with predictable resource needs. In exchange for committing to a continuous level of vCPU and memory for a 1-year or 3-year term, Google provides substantial discounts off on-demand rates.

practice_questions.stem: A software team wants to build a lightweight API microservice that receives unpredictable HTTP webhooks. Traffic fluctuates from zero requests at night to hundreds per second during peak bursts. The team wants zero server management and minimal costs during idle periods. Which Google Cloud compute service should you recommend?

options.text: Compute Engine VM with an autoscaled Managed Instance Group (MIG).
options.explanation: MIGs incur baseline cost for running VMs and take minutes to scale from zero.

options.text: Cloud Run
options.explanation: Correct. Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that deploys stateless containers, scales automatically from zero to thousands of instances based on incoming HTTP requests, and charges only for processing time per 100ms.

options.text: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard with 3 nodes.
options.explanation: GKE Standard incurs fixed 24/7 costs for cluster management and node pool VMs.

options.text: App Engine Flexible Environment.
options.explanation: App Engine Flexible requires at least 1 running VM instance and does not scale to zero.

practice_questions.explanation: Cloud Run is purpose-built for containerized HTTP microservices with dynamic traffic. It automatically scales to zero when there is no traffic (eliminating idle cost) and scales out rapidly to meet traffic spikes.

practice_questions.stem: You need to store financial transaction records for compliance auditing. The records must be retained for exactly 7 years. The data will be accessed less than once a year, but when retrieved, it must be available within milliseconds. Which Cloud Storage class should you use?

options.text: Standard Storage
options.explanation: Standard storage has the highest storage cost per GB, making it cost-ineffective for archival data accessed once a year.

options.text: Nearline Storage
options.explanation: Nearline storage is designed for data accessed once a month (30-day minimum retention).

options.text: Archive Storage
options.explanation: Correct. Archive Storage offers the lowest storage cost (for data accessed less than once a year, with 365-day minimum duration) while still providing sub-second (millisecond) retrieval latency, unlike cold storage on other cloud providers.

options.text: Cloud Bigtable
options.explanation: Bigtable is an expensive high-throughput NoSQL database, not an object archive service.

practice_questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Archive class is engineered for long-term digital preservation and regulatory compliance. It offers the lowest cost per GB and still delivers millisecond time-to-first-byte when accessed.

practice_questions.stem:
You have a custom VPC network with multiple subnets. You create two firewall rules:
Rule A: Priority 1000, Action: ALLOW, Protocol: TCP port 80, Source: 0.0.0.0/0, Target Tag: `web-server`
Rule B: Priority 500, Action: DENY, Protocol: TCP port 80, Source: 192.168.1.0/24, Target Tag: `web-server`

A client with IP 192.168.1.50 sends an HTTP request on port 80 to a VM tagged `web-server`. What will happen?

options.text: The request is ALLOWED because Rule A has a higher numeric priority value.
options.explanation: In Google Cloud VPC firewall rules, lower numbers denote higher priority (0 is highest priority, 65535 is lowest).

options.text: The request is DENIED because Rule B has priority 500, which takes precedence over Rule A (priority 1000).
options.explanation: Correct. Google Cloud firewall rules evaluate in order of priority from lowest numerical value (0) to highest (65535). Since 500 < 1000, Rule B is evaluated first and denies the connection immediately.

options.text: The request is dropped because custom VPC networks do not support tags.
options.explanation: Target tags and network tags are fully supported on custom VPC networks.

options.text: The request is ALLOWED because ALLOW rules always override DENY rules regardless of priority.
options.explanation: Rule priority strictly determines evaluation order; action type does not supersede priority ranking.

practice_questions.explanation: Firewall rule priority values range from 0 to 65535, with lower numbers representing higher priority. Evaluation terminates upon the first matching rule, so Rule B (priority 500) overrides Rule A (priority 1000).

practice_questions.stem: You need to create a Compute Engine VM that automatically downloads software packages and configures a web server on first boot. How should you supply this automation using the gcloud CLI?

options.text: Pass the bash script to the `--metadata=startup-script=...` or `--metadata-from-file=startup-script=...` flag during `gcloud compute instances create`.
options.explanation: Correct. Startup scripts specified in instance metadata are automatically executed as root by the Compute Engine guest environment when the VM powers on.

options.text: Connect via SSH after the VM is created and paste the script manually into the terminal.
options.explanation: Manual SSH execution does not provide automated deployment and cannot be used in autoscaled instance templates.

options.text: Upload the script to a Cloud Storage bucket and configure Cloud Scheduler to trigger it.
options.explanation: Cloud Scheduler triggers HTTP endpoints or Pub/Sub topics, not arbitrary local VM shell scripts without guest agent hooks.

options.text: Embed the script in the OS Login public key description.
options.explanation: OS Login manages Linux user authentication, not startup configuration.

practice_questions.explanation: Compute Engine supports `startup-script` metadata keys (or `startup-script-url` to load from Google Cloud Storage) to automate package installation, daemon configuration, and environment setup on boot.

practice_questions.stem: Your company is deploying a containerized application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You want Google to manage node provisioning, cluster scaling, security hardening, and OS updates so that your engineers only focus on deploying Pods. Which GKE cluster operational mode should you choose?

options.text: GKE Standard mode with custom node pools
options.explanation: Standard mode requires the administrator to select machine types, manage node pools, and configure OS upgrades.

options.text: GKE Autopilot mode
options.explanation: Correct. In Autopilot mode, Google provisions and manages all underlying node infrastructure based on pod resource specifications, enforces security best practices, and automates cluster maintenance.

options.text: Standalone Kubernetes on Compute Engine VMs
options.explanation: Self-managed Kubernetes has the highest administrative overhead.

options.text: Anthos Service Mesh on bare metal
options.explanation: Anthos/GKE Enterprise on bare metal is intended for on-premises hybrid deployments.

practice_questions.explanation: GKE Autopilot is a fully managed operational mode where Google manages the cluster architecture, node provisioning, and scaling according to Pod resource specifications.

practice_questions.stem: You have deployed a Cloud Run service called `payment-api`. During high-volume marketing campaigns, sudden traffic spikes cause a latency spike due to container initialization (cold starts). How can you eliminate cold starts for critical requests while remaining serverless?

options.text: Configure the `--min-instances` flag to at least 1 or more on the Cloud Run service.
options.explanation: Correct. Setting `min-instances` keeps the specified number of container instances warm and ready in memory to process requests immediately without cold start delays.

options.text: Migrate the application to App Engine Standard with 0 instances.
options.explanation: App Engine Standard with 0 instances will still experience cold starts upon receiving requests.

options.text: Decrease the `--concurrency` parameter to 1.
options.explanation: Reducing concurrency forces Cloud Run to spin up more instances for simultaneous requests, worsening cold starts.

options.text: Enable CPU allocation only during request processing.
options.explanation: Allocating CPU only during requests is the default behavior and does not keep idle instances warm.

practice_questions.explanation: Setting `--min-instances` guarantees that a baseline number of container instances stay running, eliminating cold-start latency for incoming traffic bursts.

practice_questions.stem: You are setting up a production PostgreSQL database on Cloud SQL. You must ensure that the database can automatically fail over to another availability zone within the same region with zero data loss in the event of a datacenter outage. What setting is required?

options.text: Enable High Availability (Regional availability type).
options.explanation: Correct. High Availability in Cloud SQL provisions a primary and standby instance in two separate zones in the same region, using synchronous storage replication for automatic failover without data loss.

options.text: Configure a cross-region read replica and promote it manually.
options.explanation: Manual replica promotion across regions is asynchronous and incurs failover downtime and potential data lag.

options.text: Take manual on-demand snapshots every hour.
options.explanation: Snapshots provide backup recovery points, not automated sub-minute failover.

options.text: Deploy Cloud SQL in Zonal availability with read replicas.
options.explanation: Zonal availability does not provide standby failover instances across zones.

practice_questions.explanation: Cloud SQL High Availability (HA) configuration provisions a standby instance in another zone. Synchronous replication keeps standby data identical, and automated failover activates if the primary zone becomes unreachable.

practice_questions.stem: You need to perform maintenance on a Compute Engine VM instance and change its machine type from `e2-standard-2` to `e2-standard-8`. What steps must you follow in sequence?

options.text: Stop the VM instance -> Modify the machine type -> Start the VM instance.
options.explanation: Correct. Compute Engine machine types can only be modified while the instance is in the `TERMINATED` (STOPPED) state. Once reconfigured, start the instance.

options.text: Modify the machine type on the live running instance with `gcloud compute instances update`.
options.explanation: Compute Engine does not support dynamic live resizing of vCPU/RAM on a running instance.

options.text: Delete the VM instance -> Recreate a new VM instance with the desired machine type from scratch.
options.explanation: Deleting the instance is destructive and unnecessary when attached boot disks can simply be stopped and reconfigured.

options.text: Suspend the VM instance -> Change machine type -> Resume the instance.
options.explanation: Suspended VMs preserve RAM state to disk and cannot resume on a different CPU/RAM topology.

practice_questions.explanation: To change machine attributes such as vCPU count or memory, the instance must be stopped (`gcloud compute instances stop`), updated (`set-machine-type`), and restarted.

practice_questions.stem: A recent deployment of your application to a GKE cluster caused error rates to spike. You need to immediately roll back the deployment `frontend-app` to the previous stable revision. Which kubectl command should you run?

options.text: kubectl rollout undo deployment/frontend-app
options.explanation: Correct. `kubectl rollout undo` rolls back the Deployment to the previous revision in its rollout history.

options.text: kubectl delete deployment frontend-app
options.explanation: Deleting the deployment terminates all application pods and causes complete service outage.

options.text: kubectl scale deployment frontend-app --replicas=0
options.explanation: Scaling replicas to 0 stops all pods instead of restoring the previous working version.

options.text: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --force
options.explanation: Reapplying the same manifest does not revert to the prior revision unless the YAML image tag is changed.

practice_questions.explanation: Kubernetes tracks deployment revision history. `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` rolls back to the immediate previous revision, ensuring rapid incident recovery.

practice_questions.stem: You have deployed a new revision `v2` of a Cloud Run microservice. You want to test `v2` with 10% of live customer traffic while routing the remaining 90% to the stable `v1` revision. How should you configure this?

options.text: Deploy two separate Cloud Run services and use Cloud DNS round-robin weighted records.
options.explanation: Cloud DNS does not natively support weighted percentage routing.

options.text: Use Cloud Run Traffic Splitting to allocate 10% traffic to revision `v2` and 90% to revision `v1`.
options.explanation: Correct. Cloud Run has built-in traffic splitting that routes incoming HTTP requests across revisions based on user-defined percentages.

options.text: Create a Cloud Function proxy that randomly redirects 10% of requests via HTTP 302.
options.explanation: HTTP redirects add client latency and complicate client-side cookie/header handling.

options.text: Set `v2` instance concurrency to 10 and `v1` concurrency to 90.
options.explanation: Concurrency controls simultaneous requests per container, not traffic routing distribution.

practice_questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports native traffic splitting (`gcloud run services update-traffic`) between multiple revisions, enabling safe canary releases and gradual rollouts.

practice_questions.stem: Security compliance requires all Cloud Audit Logs and system error logs across your organization to be retained for 5 years for forensic analysis, and made queryable via SQL. Cloud Logging default retention is 30 days. What is the recommended solution?

options.text: Create a Log Router sink in Cloud Logging with a destination of BigQuery, and set the BigQuery dataset table partition expiration to 5 years.
options.explanation: Correct. Log Router sinks continuously stream log entries matching filter criteria to BigQuery, where standard SQL queries and long-term retention policies can be configured.

options.text: Write a bash script in Cloud Shell that runs `gcloud logging read` daily and saves files to local storage.
options.explanation: Manual scripts in Cloud Shell are not durable, scalable, or compliant.

options.text: Increase Cloud Logging `_Default` bucket retention to 5 years in the console.
options.explanation: Cloud Logging log bucket custom retention can be set up to 10 years, but does not provide direct ANSI SQL querying capabilities like BigQuery does.

options.text: Stream logs to Cloud Pub/Sub and discard messages after ACK.
options.explanation: Pub/Sub is a temporary message queue with maximum 7-day retention, not a storage solution.

practice_questions.explanation: Cloud Logging Log Router sinks allow exporting log entries in real time to BigQuery datasets, enabling long-term compliance storage and SQL analytics.

practice_questions.stem: You need to grant a junior engineer access to start and stop VM instances in a development project, but prevent them from deleting VMs, modifying firewall rules, or accessing Cloud Storage. Following the principle of least privilege, what should you do?

options.text: Grant the primitive `roles/editor` role on the project.
options.explanation: The primitive Editor role grants broad modification and deletion privileges across almost all services in the project.

options.text: Create a custom IAM role containing only `compute.instances.start`, `compute.instances.stop`, and `compute.instances.get` permissions, and bind it to the engineer's identity.
options.explanation: Correct. When no predefined role matches the exact granular restriction required, creating a Custom Role with specific permissions enforces the principle of least privilege.

options.text: Grant the predefined `roles/compute.admin` role on the project.
options.explanation: Compute Admin grants full control over compute instances, firewalls, and networks, violating least privilege.

options.text: Grant the primitive `roles/viewer` role and assign SSH key metadata.
options.explanation: Viewer role is read-only and does not allow starting or stopping instances.

practice_questions.explanation: Custom IAM roles allow curating exact permission sets when predefined roles are too broad, satisfying strict least-privilege compliance.

practice_questions.stem: Your CI/CD pipeline running in GitHub Actions needs to deploy container images to Google Cloud Artifact Registry and update Cloud Run services. You want to authenticate securely without storing static, downloadable JSON service account keys in GitHub Secrets. What is the recommended security architecture?

options.text: Configure Workload Identity Federation between GitHub Actions and Google Cloud IAM.
options.explanation: Correct. Workload Identity Federation exchanges OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity tokens from GitHub Actions for short-lived Google Cloud access tokens, completely eliminating long-lived service account keys.

options.text: Generate a service account private key in JSON format, base64 encode it, and store it in GitHub repository secrets.
options.explanation: Storing static JSON keys in external secret stores is a security risk because keys do not expire automatically and can be leaked.

options.text: Hardcode the service account email and password in the GitHub Actions workflow YAML file.
options.explanation: Service accounts do not use passwords, and hardcoding credentials in repository code is unsafe.

options.text: Assign the GitHub Actions runner an external IP and add it to the Google Cloud authorized network list.
options.explanation: IP whitelisting does not perform cryptographic identity authentication.

practice_questions.explanation: Workload Identity Federation allows external workloads (GitHub Actions, AWS, Azure) to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs using short-lived credentials, eliminating the operational and security risks of service account keys.

practice_questions.stem: You are investigating an incident where a confidential Cloud Storage bucket had objects read by an unauthorized entity. You check Cloud Logging for Data Access audit logs, but find no log entries for the read requests. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Data Access audit logs (except for BigQuery) are disabled by default to save storage costs and must be explicitly enabled in IAM audit configuration.
options.explanation: Correct. Admin Activity audit logs are always enabled and free, but Data Access audit logs (which record read/write operations on user data) are disabled by default due to high volume and must be explicitly activated.

options.text: Cloud Storage does not support audit logging.
options.explanation: Cloud Storage fully supports both Admin Activity and Data Access audit logging.

options.text: Audit logs are deleted immediately after 24 hours.
options.explanation: Admin Activity logs are retained for 400 days; Data Access logs are retained for 30 days by default.

options.text: Only project Owners can view audit logs.
options.explanation: Users with `roles/logging.viewer` or `roles/logging.privateLogViewer` can view audit logs.

practice_questions.explanation: Data Access audit logs record API calls that read or write user-provided resource data. Because of high log volume, Data Access logs (Admin Read, Data Read, Data Write) are disabled by default for most services and require explicit activation in the IAM Audit Configuration.
